COM747 Week 9: Association Rule Mining

Lecture demonstrations and complete seminar solutions

How to use this notebook. Part A computes support, confidence and lift by hand on a tiny shop so the formulas are concrete, and shows the apriori pruning idea. Part B is the complete seminar exercise on the Groceries data (Exercise(6).pdf / exercise(2).pptx), with every step answered. Part C is extra practice. The data is built into arules, so no files are needed.

library(arules)       # transactions, apriori(), inspect()
library(arulesViz)    # plot() methods for rules

Part A: The measures by hand

A1. The lecture example (3 baskets)

baskets <- list(
  c("milk", "bread", "eggs", "apples", "grapes"),
  c("carrots", "peas", "potatoes"),
  c("carrots", "peas", "potatoes", "milk", "bread", "eggs"))
trans <- as(baskets, "transactions")    # convert a list of baskets to the arules class
inspect(trans)
##     items                                       
## [1] {apples, bread, eggs, grapes, milk}         
## [2] {carrots, peas, potatoes}                   
## [3] {bread, carrots, eggs, milk, peas, potatoes}
as(trans, "matrix") * 1                 # the 0/1 basket-by-item matrix behind it
##      apples bread carrots eggs grapes milk peas potatoes
## [1,]      1     1       0    1      1    1    0        0
## [2,]      0     0       1    0      0    0    1        1
## [3,]      0     1       1    1      0    1    1        1
N <- length(trans)
has <- function(item) sapply(baskets, function(b) all(item %in% b))   # TRUE if basket contains every item

support    <- function(items) sum(has(items)) / N
confidence <- function(lhs, rhs) support(c(lhs, rhs)) / support(lhs)
lift       <- function(lhs, rhs) confidence(lhs, rhs) / support(rhs)

support("milk")                    # 2/3: as on the slide
## [1] 0.6666667
support(c("milk", "bread"))        # 2/3: the support of the rule {milk} => {bread}
## [1] 0.6666667
confidence("milk", "bread")        # 1: every basket with milk has bread
## [1] 1
lift("milk", "bread")              # 1 / (2/3) = 1.5
## [1] 1.5

Ask (slide question): which items should the algorithm ignore? Apples and grapes appear in only one basket of three, so with a minimum support of, say, 0.5 they can be dropped before any pairs are considered.

A2. Check with apriori()

r <- apriori(trans, parameter = list(support = 0.5, confidence = 0.5, minlen = 2),
             control = list(verbose = FALSE))
inspect(subset(r, lhs %in% "milk" & rhs %in% "bread"))   # support 0.67, confidence 1, lift 1.5
##     lhs             rhs     support   confidence coverage  lift count
## [1] {milk}       => {bread} 0.6666667 1          0.6666667 1.5  2    
## [2] {eggs, milk} => {bread} 0.6666667 1          0.6666667 1.5  2

A3. Why lift matters: a 10-basket shop

shop <- list(c("bread","milk","eggs"), c("bread","butter"), c("milk","nappies","beer"),
             c("bread","milk","butter"), c("bread","milk","eggs","butter"), c("beer","nappies"),
             c("milk","eggs"), c("bread","milk","beer","nappies"), c("bread","eggs","butter"),
             c("milk","nappies","beer"))
shopT <- as(shop, "transactions")
itemFrequency(shopT)                     # milk is in 7 of 10 baskets
##    beer   bread  butter    eggs    milk nappies 
##     0.4     0.6     0.4     0.4     0.7     0.4
shopRules <- apriori(shopT, parameter = list(support = 0.2, confidence = 0.5, minlen = 2),
                     control = list(verbose = FALSE))
inspect(sort(shopRules, by = "lift")[1:5])
##     lhs                rhs       support confidence coverage lift     count
## [1] {beer}          => {nappies} 0.4     1          0.4      2.500000 4    
## [2] {nappies}       => {beer}    0.4     1          0.4      2.500000 4    
## [3] {beer, milk}    => {nappies} 0.3     1          0.3      2.500000 3    
## [4] {milk, nappies} => {beer}    0.3     1          0.3      2.500000 3    
## [5] {butter}        => {bread}   0.4     1          0.4      1.666667 4
inspect(subset(shopRules, rhs %in% "milk"))
##     lhs                rhs    support confidence coverage lift      count
## [1] {eggs}          => {milk} 0.3     0.7500000  0.4      1.0714286 3    
## [2] {butter}        => {milk} 0.2     0.5000000  0.4      0.7142857 2    
## [3] {beer}          => {milk} 0.3     0.7500000  0.4      1.0714286 3    
## [4] {nappies}       => {milk} 0.3     0.7500000  0.4      1.0714286 3    
## [5] {bread}         => {milk} 0.4     0.6666667  0.6      0.9523810 4    
## [6] {bread, eggs}   => {milk} 0.2     0.6666667  0.3      0.9523810 2    
## [7] {bread, butter} => {milk} 0.2     0.5000000  0.4      0.7142857 2    
## [8] {beer, nappies} => {milk} 0.3     0.7500000  0.4      1.0714286 3

Ask: {eggs} ⇒ {milk} has confidence 0.75. Is that a good rule? Milk is in 70% of all baskets anyway, so lift is only 0.75 / 0.7 ≈ 1.07: eggs tell us almost nothing about milk. {nappies} ⇒ {beer} has lift 2.5.

A4. The combinatorial explosion and the apriori property

k <- c(5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 169)
data.frame(items = k, possible_itemsets = format(2^k, scientific = TRUE, digits = 4))
##   items possible_itemsets
## 1     5         3.200e+01
## 2    10         1.024e+03
## 3    20         1.049e+06
## 4    50         1.126e+15
## 5   100         1.268e+30
## 6   169         7.483e+50
2^100                                    # 1.267651e+30, as on the slide
## [1] 1.267651e+30

The apriori property: every subset of a frequent itemset must also be frequent. So candidates of size k are only built from frequent itemsets of size k − 1. Here is the level-by-level search written out for the 10-basket shop with a minimum count of 3:

items <- itemLabels(shopT)
count <- function(s) sum(sapply(shop, function(b) all(s %in% b)))
min_count <- 3

level <- lapply(items, identity)            # level 1: every single item
k <- 1
while (length(level) > 0) {
  counts   <- sapply(level, count)
  frequent <- level[counts >= min_count]
  cat("Level", k, ": counted", length(level), "candidates,", length(frequent), "frequent\n")
  if (length(frequent) > 0) print(sapply(frequent, paste, collapse = ","))
  if (length(frequent) < 2) break           # nothing left to combine
  # build size k+1 candidates from frequent itemsets, keeping only those whose
  # every size-k subset is frequent (the apriori pruning step)
  cand <- unique(lapply(combn(length(frequent), 2, simplify = FALSE),
                        function(ij) sort(unique(c(frequent[[ij[1]]], frequent[[ij[2]]])))))
  cand <- Filter(function(s) length(s) == k + 1, cand)
  key  <- sapply(frequent, paste, collapse = ",")
  cand <- Filter(function(s) all(combn(s, k, paste, collapse = ",") %in% key), cand)
  level <- cand; k <- k + 1
}
## Level 1 : counted 6 candidates, 6 frequent
## [1] "beer"    "bread"   "butter"  "eggs"    "milk"    "nappies"
## Level 2 : counted 15 candidates, 7 frequent
## [1] "beer,milk"    "beer,nappies" "bread,butter" "bread,eggs"   "bread,milk"  
## [6] "eggs,milk"    "milk,nappies"
## Level 3 : counted 2 candidates, 1 frequent
## [1] "beer,milk,nappies"

B2. Check the support of the top 5 items

Support is how often an item occurs: count / number of transactions.

top5_counts <- c("whole milk" = 2513, "other vegetables" = 1903, "rolls/buns" = 1809,
                 "soda" = 1715, "yogurt" = 1372)
round(top5_counts / length(Groceries), 4)                       # by hand

B4. Sparsity

image(Groceries[1:200])       # rows = first 200 transactions, columns = 169 items

Almost everything is white: each basket holds a handful of the 169 items. The vertical streaks are the popular items (whole milk, other vegetables…). A random sample is a fairer picture than the first 200 rows:

set.seed(1)
image(sample(Groceries, 100))

B5. Run apriori

rules <- apriori(Groceries, parameter = list(support = 0.001, confidence = 0.25, minlen = 2))
## Apriori
## 
## Parameter specification:
##  confidence minval smax arem  aval originalSupport maxtime support minlen
##        0.25    0.1    1 none FALSE            TRUE       5   0.001      2
##  maxlen target  ext
##      10  rules TRUE
## 
## Algorithmic control:
##  filter tree heap memopt load sort verbose
##     0.1 TRUE TRUE  FALSE TRUE    2    TRUE
## 
## Absolute minimum support count: 9 
## 
## set item appearances ...[0 item(s)] done [0.00s].
## set transactions ...[169 item(s), 9835 transaction(s)] done [0.00s].
## sorting and recoding items ... [157 item(s)] done [0.00s].
## creating transaction tree ... done [0.00s].
## checking subsets of size 1 2 3 4 5 6 done [0.01s].
## writing ... [17391 rule(s)] done [0.00s].
## creating S4 object  ... done [0.00s].
rules
## set of 17391 rules
  • support = 0.001: an itemset must appear in at least 0.1% of baskets (≈ 10 baskets).
  • confidence = 0.25: the rule must be right at least 25% of the time.
  • minlen = 2: at least two items in the rule, so no empty-LHS rules like {} => {whole milk}.

Different limits give very different numbers of rules:

grid <- expand.grid(support = c(0.001, 0.005, 0.01), confidence = c(0.25, 0.5))
grid$rules <- mapply(function(s, c) length(apriori(Groceries,
  parameter = list(support = s, confidence = c, minlen = 2), control = list(verbose = FALSE))),
  grid$support, grid$confidence)
grid
##   support confidence rules
## 1   0.001       0.25 17391
## 2   0.005       0.25   662
## 3   0.010       0.25   170
## 4   0.001       0.50  5668
## 5   0.005       0.50   120
## 6   0.010       0.50    15

B7. Check the lift by hand

supp_milk <- itemFrequency(Groceries)["whole milk"]
supp_milk                                 # 0.255516
## whole milk 
##   0.255516
0.7333333 / 0.255516                      # 2.870009, the slide's calculation
## [1] 2.870009
q <- quality(rules[1])
q$confidence / supp_milk                  # same, from the rule object
## whole milk 
##   2.870009
q$lift
## [1] 2.870009
# Check all 20 at once: lift = confidence / support(rhs)
r20 <- rules[1:20]
rhs_items <- unlist(LIST(rhs(r20)))
check <- data.frame(rule = labels(r20),
                    confidence = quality(r20)$confidence,
                    supp_rhs   = itemFrequency(Groceries)[rhs_items],
                    lift_by_hand = quality(r20)$confidence / itemFrequency(Groceries)[rhs_items],
                    lift_arules  = quality(r20)$lift, row.names = NULL)
check[, -1] <- round(check[, -1], 4)
check

Ask: Each sort tells a different story. Sorting by support shows what is common (but obvious); by confidence shows rules that are always right (but often just predict the most popular item); by lift shows what is surprising. Which one would a store manager want? Usually lift, with a minimum support so the rule affects enough customers.

Two useful extras: remove redundant rules (a longer rule that is no better than a shorter one), and subset by item.

rules_nr <- rules[!is.redundant(rules)]
length(rules); length(rules_nr)
## [1] 17391
## [1] 15118
inspect(sort(subset(rules, rhs %in% "bottled beer"), by = "lift")[1:5])

B10. Plot the rules

plot(rules)                                       # support vs confidence, shaded by lift

plot(sort(rules, by = "confidence")[1:200])

plot() for rules comes from arulesViz. Without library(arulesViz) loaded, plot(rules) fails, so the sheet’s order (plot first, install arulesViz afterwards) needs swapping: load it first.

B11. arulesViz graphs

# With all 17,391 rules arulesViz only draws the best 100 (by lift), with a warning
plot(rules, method = "graph", measure = "confidence", shading = "support")

plot(sort(rules, by = "confidence")[1:30], method = "graph", measure = "lift", shading = "confidence")

Circles are rules; arrows point from LHS items into a rule and from the rule to its RHS item. Circle size shows the measure, colour the shading. Nearly all arrows end at whole milk or other vegetables.

plot(sort(rules, by = "lift")[1:50], method = "grouped")    # LHS groups vs RHS items

Part C: Extra practice

C1. Your own data with read.transactions()

# Write a small basket file: one transaction per line, items separated by commas
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
writeLines(c("bread,milk,eggs", "bread,butter", "milk,nappies,beer", "bread,milk,butter"), tmp)
myT <- read.transactions(tmp, format = "basket", sep = ",")
inspect(myT)
##     items                
## [1] {bread, eggs, milk}  
## [2] {bread, butter}      
## [3] {beer, milk, nappies}
## [4] {bread, butter, milk}

C2. Classify some rules

top <- sort(rules[!is.redundant(rules)], by = "lift")[1:8]
inspect(top)
##     lhs                                rhs                support    
## [1] {bottled beer, red/blush wine}  => {liquor}           0.001931876
## [2] {ham, white bread}              => {processed cheese} 0.001931876
## [3] {bottled beer, liquor}          => {red/blush wine}   0.001931876
## [4] {Instant food products, soda}   => {hamburger meat}   0.001220132
## [5] {curd, sugar}                   => {flour}            0.001118454
## [6] {sugar, baking powder}          => {flour}            0.001016777
## [7] {processed cheese, white bread} => {ham}              0.001931876
## [8] {ham, fruit/vegetable juice}    => {processed cheese} 0.001118454
##     confidence coverage    lift     count
## [1] 0.3958333  0.004880529 35.71579 19   
## [2] 0.3800000  0.005083884 22.92822 19   
## [3] 0.4130435  0.004677173 21.49356 19   
## [4] 0.6315789  0.001931876 18.99565 12   
## [5] 0.3235294  0.003457041 18.60767 11   
## [6] 0.3125000  0.003253686 17.97332 10   
## [7] 0.4634146  0.004168785 17.80345 19   
## [8] 0.2894737  0.003863752 17.46610 11

Discussion (Lantz’s three categories):

  • Trivial: {bottled beer, red/blush wine} ⇒ {liquor}: alcohol is bought together; no surprise.
  • Actionable: {herbs} ⇒ {root vegetables} (lift ≈ 4.0, 69 baskets): cooking ingredients; place together or bundle a recipe promotion.
  • Inexplicable: a rule such as {Instant food products, soda} ⇒ {hamburger meat} could be a promotion that month, a single large customer, or chance among thousands of rules. Investigate before acting.

Load data("Groceries"), read.transactions(file, format = "basket", sep = ",")
Explore summary(), itemFrequency(), itemFrequencyPlot(topN, support), image()

Inspect inspect(rules[1:20]), quality(rules), size(rules)
Rank and filter sort(rules, by = "lift"), subset(rules, rhs %in% "x" & lift > 3), is.redundant()
